findings.interpretation: The response was military, with civilian mariner reporting and regional coordination essential. Neither source attributes success to a naval battle or establishes blanket protection.
findings.observation: The September10 GLAMOR incident was resolved through merchant-crew protective action and a military-led multinational response. ATALANTA redirected assets; Republic of Korea-led CTF151 coordinated a Japanese maritime patrol aircraft and information sharing with ATALANTA, the Indian Navy and regional agencies. Pirates left; the crew was safe and the vessel resumed transit.

findings.interpretation: Actual physical flow reductions are established in a dated estimate; a uniform blockade around the whole Arabian Peninsula is not established. This is one supply event shared with fuel_cover, not a second independent shock.
findings.observation: IEA September11 public report estimates August Gulf oil exports near13 million barrels/day, almost half prewar. It describes severely constrained Hormuz flows, US military escorts and increased bypass flows, alongside renewed attacks at Bab el-Mandeb.

findings.interpretation: Mandates overlap geographically but are not interchangeable. The same ship cannot be assumed available to every task force or every threat.
findings.observation: ATALANTA combines anti-piracy and vulnerable-vessel protection with other maritime-security tasks. CTF151 has a counter-piracy mission and coordinates with EUNAVFOR. ASPIDES is a distinct defensive shipping-protection operation associated with the Red Sea crisis, extended to February28,2027.

findings.interpretation: No public deployment order or matched before/after coverage evidence was verified showing current Hormuz/Red Sea operations depleted piracy response elsewhere. Successful September response is counterevidence to a claim that response has ceased; it does not settle overall adequacy.
findings.observation: Combat protection, escorts and counter-piracy can compete for ships, aircraft, crews and maintenance time if contributing countries reassign the same assets.

findings.interpretation: Trace origin, cargo type, route and destination separately. A price spike or reduced Gulf export flow alone cannot quantify additional waiting time at a particular East Asian refinery.
findings.observation: Eastbound Gulf-to-East-Asia cargo exits through Hormuz; it need not pass through Bab el-Mandeb. Supplies sourced through Suez/Red Sea face a different route constraint. Atlantic replacements may require longer voyages and suitable refinery feedstock.

resilience.commons: Shared bulk ordering can consolidate essential demand and publish replenishment windows without assuming every organization can purchase at spot prices.
resilience.falsifier: Normal timely deliveries plus adequate accessible stocks would downgrade a predicted downstream interruption; documented reassignment plus reduced response coverage would support the currently unproven diversion mechanism.
resilience.growth: Route-diverse procurement, inventory visibility, port coordination, appropriate electric local logistics, efficient fuel use and regional maritime cooperation.
resilience.lifeboat: A rotating critical-fuel allocation and essential delivery service that can operate until a realistic replenishment arrival; donor and recipient clocks both matter.
resilience.release: Postpone discretionary fuel-intensive activity or nonessential shipments while preserving food, healthcare and repair logistics; do not exhaust donor essentials.
resilience.reserve: Accessible compatible inventories, tankage and refinable feedstock can bridge waiting; each needs days-of-cover at essential-use demand, withdrawal rate and protected domestic floor. No new country inventory quantified by this thread.
resilience.substitution: Alternate crude/product origins, legal commercial swaps, usable bypass routes and compatible local refining. Swapping ownership does not create molecules; refinery nameplate is not operable spare capacity.

response_time_model.decision_rule: A substitute can bridge the gap only if useful delivery or production begins before essential-service stocks are exhausted, at sufficient rate. A one-off inventory draw does not fix a persistent inflow deficit.
